newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian wages point to moderate inflation.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian wages point to moderate inflation.

text.p: Contained private sector wages growth has further confirmed the favourable prospects for Australia's 1997 inflation outlook, economists said on Thursday.

The moderate growth in private average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE), following on from Wednesday's news of some slowing in the pace of enterprise bargaining agreements, was seen as further evidence that official rates were on hold.
Data released on Thursday confirmed preliminary data from earlier this month showing AWOTE rose 1.2 percent in the three months to November, to be up 3.9 percent over the year.
Bankers Trust chief economist Chris Caton described the data as "roaringly good numbers" but he added that "it doesn't mean the Reserve Bank is going to say it will cut rates again."
Of most interest to economists in the final figures was the pace of wages growth in the private sector.
They rose 0.8 percent in the quarter to be up 2.8 percent over the year, down from 3.5 percent in the year to August.

"The further slowing in private sector wages growth, down from a peak of 6.1 percent at the end of 1995, provides further confirmation of the favourable inflation outlook for 1997," Commonwealth Bank senior economist Michael Blythe said.

In its quarterly report on the economy released last week, the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA), while acknowleding that wages remained the main uncertainty on the inflation outlook, forecast underlying inflation to remain around two percent in 1997, and for it to be in the two to three percent band in 1998.

Thursday's moderation in the annual pace of growth in private sector AWOTE followed Wednesday's release of data showing the annualised rate of increase in new enterprise agreements had eased to 4.4 percent in the December quarter from 5.3 percent in the September quarter.
"I like the private sector outcome," Dresdner Australia chief economist Rob Henderson said.
"Coming on top of the figures we got yesterday on enterprise bargaining, I think the inflation outlook is excellent."

But while the outlook was positive, given signs of stronger activity and some uncertainties over wages in 1997, including the outcome of the union movement's "living wage" claim, the RBA was most likely to leave interest rates steady, economists said.
While private sector wages were moderating, public sector wages retained the strength that has seen them rise by more than the private sector in each quarter of 1996.
Public sector AWOTE rose 2.2 percent in the quarter, following on from a 2.5 percent rise in the August quarter, which saw them up 7.6 percent over the year.

However, these figures may have been affected by compositional changes to the public service which have seen the measure of average wages rise, even though pay increases of that magnitude had not been granted.
The RBA last week said the recent strength in public sector wages was unusual as the bulk of enterprise bargains were for increases of about four percent.

The RBA said this might be the result of a compositional change in public sector employment if recent cutbacks had mainly affected lower income earners. If this was so, it may not then be appropriate to draw strong conclusions from the data.

Economists agreed that structural changes to the public sector appeared to be affecting the outcome, and said in any case private sector wages were more important in terms of the impact of wages on inflation.
"In terms of inflation its the private sector that has a direct impact on costs and hence consumer prices," Dresdner's Henderson said. -- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373 1800
